title: Shammai's measuring stick (Shabbat 31a)
hook: the same man went first to Shammai, who pushed him away with a builder's rod

segments.voice: Yesterday Hillel gave the whole Torah on one foot. Your line was the rest is commentary. Did you catch yourself before doing the thing that stings? Day two hundred seventy-three.

Here's the part of yesterday's story that usually gets cut. Before the man ever reached Hillel, he went to someone else. He knocked on the door of Shammai, the other great sage of the generation, and asked the same thing: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. Shammai had a builder's measuring rod in his hand. And he pushed the man away with it. Only then did the man walk across town to Hillel. Today, the measuring stick, and why the Talmud bothers to tell us about it.
screen: `FIRST HE KNOCKED ON SHAMMAI'S DOOR.` → `A BUILDER'S ROD IN HIS HAND.` → `PUSHED AWAY.`

segments.voice: The Talmud calls it the builder's cubit, a straight rod for measuring. It's a perfect picture. Shammai measured things exactly, and a question that didn't measure up got pushed out the door. The same page tells two more stories like it. One man wants to accept only the written Torah, not the oral teaching. Another wants to convert so he can become high priest. Each time Shammai sends him away, and each time Hillel takes him in, and teaches him patiently until the man sees for himself. Right before these stories, the Talmud tells of a man who bet four hundred coins that he could make Hillel lose his temper. He knocked on Hillel's door on Friday afternoon, while Hillel was washing for Shabbat, and asked silly questions. Why are Babylonians' heads round? Hillel came out, answered kindly, and went back in. Again and again. The man lost his bet. So the Talmud draws a lesson: a person should always be humble and patient like Hillel, and not strict and impatient like Shammai. But hold on. Shammai isn't a villain. He was one of the great teachers, and his school's rulings fill the Mishnah. His own famous saying, in Pirkei Avot, is to receive every person with a cheerful face. Maybe that was the lesson he taught himself. The measuring stick is real. So is the cheerful face.
screen: `THE BUILDER'S CUBIT.` · `THREE SEEKERS, TWO DOORS.` · `THE BET: MAKE HILLEL ANGRY.` · `SHAMMAI: A CHEERFUL FACE.` · then, large: `BE PATIENT LIKE HILLEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and a look back at this week. Settle, and breathe. We learned not to judge the jug by its outside, four kinds of people, what the Talmud is, that there's no page one, the first question, and the whole Torah on one foot. Now think of a question that tests your patience. A child's fifth why. A coworker asking the same thing again. Picture the question coming. Feel the rod in your hand. Then picture yourself putting it down, and answering the way Hillel answered, kindly, one more time. The bell holds the time.
Shammai's measuring stick. The builder's rod he used to push away a strange question, and the reason the Talmud says: be patient like Hillel.
Your line: be patient like hillel. Today, when someone asks you a strange or repeated question, put down the measuring stick and answer kindly. Day two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers often retell the stories of Hillel and Shammai together; the saying about being patient like Hillel is quoted to encourage kindness toward questioners and newcomers.

original.note: Hebrew: the builder's cubit, the measuring rod Shammai held.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shammai was the mean one.
what it means: the story asks you to put down the measuring stick when someone asks a strange question.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud's phrase is amat ha-binyan, a builder's cubit, and Shammai's own saying in Avot 1:15 is to greet everyone cheerfully.

notes: Week-end look-back covers days 267–273 (not the jug, four kinds of people, Talmud, daf, the first question, on one foot).

Shabbat 30b–31a paraphrased: the four-hundred-zuz bet, the three would-be converts, and the saying 'a person should always be humble like Hillel and not exacting like Shammai'. The Hebrew words are anvetan and kapdan; 'patient' and 'strict and impatient' are renderings.
The suggestion that Shammai's cheerful-face saying was a lesson he taught himself is an interpretive aside, marked with 'maybe'; a Keeper may prefer to drop it.
